understanding.core_struggle: Has been trying to build apps for years without success, while carrying a job, children, and ageing parents, and now questions what they are doing wrong.
understanding.mirror: You keep building on the side, and every time it does not work, the verdict falls on you alone.
understanding.insight: You are not failing at building. You are trying to build in the cracks of a life that has no cracks left, and the verdict is on the life, not on you.

queries.hook: The weight of years of trying that have not worked, and the quiet belief that you are the one who is wrong.
queries.diagnose: When a result goes wrong, the mind turns against itself; self-blame grows from believing the outcome alone measures our worth.
queries.steady: A failure is something that happened, not who you are; no one who tries to do good is ever lost, and the self that builds is not the same as the result.
queries.act: Lift yourself up instead of pushing yourself down; learn what this taught you, make amends where you can, and begin again with one small, clear step.
queries.story: A man who tried and failed, faced the verdict that he was nothing, and found the courage to begin again with one small, clear step.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse.sanskrit: कार्पण्यदोषोपहतस्वभावःपृच्छामि त्वां धर्मसंमूढचेताः । यच्छ्रेयः स्यान्निश्चितं ब्रूहि तन्मेशिष्यस्तेऽहं शाधि मां त्वां प्रपन्नम् ॥
verse.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.
verse.why: Admitting you don't know and asking for help is where clarity begins.

prasang.title: Krishna and Arjuna on Arjuna's faint-heartedness
prasang.summary: Krishna challenges Arjuna's despair. Arjuna admits he is confused about what is right, cannot tell which choice is better, and asks Krishna to teach him.
prasang.lesson: Admitting you don't know and asking for help is where clarity begins.

verse.meaning: Arjuna has stopped. He is on the battlefield, his body shaking, and he tells Krishna that his mind is clouded and he does not know what is right. He says he is ready to learn and asks Krishna to tell him plainly what is best. The verse shows that when a person admits they are lost and asks for help, clarity can begin. It is not a failure to not know. It is the beginning of the path.
verse.for_you: You have carried the question of what is wrong for years, and now your mind is tired from it. Let yourself see that not knowing is not the same as failing. You are ready to learn what is actually best for you, not just what is expected.

verse.speaker: Janaka
verse.setting: King Janaka, alone on his palace roof after overhearing wandering sages, rethinks his life.
verse.sanskrit: संपदश्च विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेच्चित्तेन संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा हन्त मन्ये महापदः ॥ आपदोऽपि विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेन्मनसि संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा मन्ये मनसि संपदः ॥
verse.line: Good fortune the mind clutches becomes trouble. Trouble the mind accepts becomes a kind of fortune.
verse.translation: All those dazzling fortunes, if the mind clings to them, are really great calamities in grand disguise. And all those varied misfortunes, if the mind accepts them, are really fortunes.
verse.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.
verse.misuse: Accepting a hardship doesn't mean not fixing what can be fixed.

prasang.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
prasang.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
prasang.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
prasang.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

verse.meaning: King Janaka sits alone on his palace roof. He has just heard wandering sages speak of a self beyond all worldly roles. The weight of his kingdom, his duties, his very identity, feels ready to crush him. But then the doorkeeper calls him to his work. Janaka decides to get up. He will not run away. He will rule, he will care for his people, he will live in the world, but with a mind that no longer clutches at fortune or fears misfortune.
verse.for_you: You keep getting up to do the work of the day. You care for your children, your parents, your job. What if the way you hold all of it could shift? You do not need to leave your life to change it. You can do the work with a mind that does not clutch.

verse.speaker: Vidula
verse.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son Sanjaya, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
verse.sanskrit: पुत्र नात्मावमन्तव्यः पूर्वाभिरसमृद्धिभिः / अभूत्वा हि भवन्त्यर्था भूत्वा नश्यन्ति चापरे / अमर्षेणैव चाप्यर्था नारब्धव्याः सुबालिशैः
verse.line: Don't look down on yourself because of past failures. Fortunes come and go, and can come again.
verse.translation: Son, don't look down on yourself because of past failures. Fortunes that never were come to be, and fortunes that were are lost. But don't start things out of mere resentment, like a fool.
verse.why: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

prasang.title: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.story_hook: A prince lay in bed after losing everything, until his mother walked in and refused to let him stay there.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

verse.meaning: Queen Vidula finds her son Sanjaya lying on the ground. He has lost his kingdom, and he believes he is finished. She tells him not to look down on himself because of what has passed. She says fortunes come and go, and those that were lost can return. But she warns him not to rise from mere resentment. He must choose to act with a clear mind, not from the sting of past defeat.
verse.for_you: Years of trying to build an app have not worked. It is natural to feel finished. But past failure does not define you. You can still choose to act, not from the sting of what went wrong, but from a clear mind that knows the next step.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: पातितोऽपि कराघातैरुत्पतत्येव कन्दुकः । प्रायेण साधुवृत्तनामस्थायिन्यो विपत्तयः ॥
verse.line: A ball knocked down bounces back up. For good people, setbacks rarely last.
verse.translation: A ball struck down by the hand flies right back up. As a rule, the misfortunes of those who live rightly do not last.
verse.why: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.
verse.misuse: Not a promise that suffering is always short, or that people who suffer long did something wrong.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to the reader from his section on steadiness. He says that a ball struck down by a hand flies right back up. As a rule, the misfortunes of those who live rightly do not last. He is telling you that setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path, and that a struck ball bounces back. He offers this to your life today as a quiet truth about what it means to keep going.
verse.for_you: You have been trying to build apps for years and the silence from the world has become heavy. Let the quiet of this evening be your struck ball. Let it land and rest, and trust that the next morning it will fly right back up.

verse.speaker: Bhishma
verse.setting: Bhishma on his bed of arrows begins teaching Yudhishthira how to lead.
verse.sanskrit: विपन्ने च समारम्भे सन्तापं मा स्म वै कृथाः / घटेतैवं सदाऽऽत्मानं राज्ञामेष परो नयः
verse.line: When something you started fails, don't torment yourself. Gather yourself and apply yourself again.
verse.translation: If an undertaking fails, do not torment yourself over it. Keep applying yourself again and again; this is the highest rule for those who lead.

matched.label: I can't tell if continuing is discipline or stubbornness

verse.meaning: Bhishma lies on his bed of arrows and tells Yudhishthira that a failed undertaking is not a reason to torment yourself. He says the highest rule for a leader is to keep applying yourself again and again. A project that falls does not mean you could stop. It means you gather your thoughts and return to the work with the same steady mind.
verse.for_you: You have spent years trying to build your app while the rest of your life asks for everything you have. This verse does not ask you to start again today. It asks you to stop tormenting yourself over what has not worked. Let the failure sit. Do not use it against yourself.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse.sanskrit: उद्धरेदात्मनाऽऽत्मानं नात्मानमवसादयेत् । आत्मैव ह्यात्मनो बन्धुरात्मैव रिपुरात्मनः ॥
verse.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.
verse.why: You can be your own best friend or worst enemy; choose friend.
verse.misuse: Not 'you're alone, so don't ask for help'. Arjuna himself asks for help; this is about not abandoning yourself.

prasang.title: Lift yourself by yourself; marks of the realised
prasang.summary: Raise yourself by yourself; you are your own friend or enemy. The self-mastered person stays calm in heat and cold, praise and blame, and sees friend and foe alike.
prasang.lesson: You can be your own best friend or worst enemy; choose friend.

verse.meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield, where Arjuna is frozen by despair and self-reproach. He tells him that the self is a person's own friend or their own enemy, and that one must lift oneself up by oneself without letting oneself sink. The verse proposes that you are the only one who can pull yourself out of this slump, because the power to change your inner state rests entirely within you, not with any outside force.
verse.for_you: You have been trying to build your apps for years while carrying a job, your children, and your parents. You do not need to prove your worth to them or to yourself today. Be your own friend. Do not push yourself down.

story.title: Hanuman's search and near despair
story.story_hook: Hanuman had searched every palace in Lanka by moonlight, and she was nowhere.
story.summary: Hanuman searches Lanka all night without finding Sita. He is close to despair, weighing what failure will mean for everyone, then tells himself that refusing to lose heart is the root of success, and searches again.
story.lesson: When you have looked everywhere, look again; giving up costs too much.

anchor.speaker: Hanuman
anchor.setting: Having searched all of Lanka without finding Sita, Hanuman fights off despair.
anchor.sanskrit: अनिर्वेदः श्रियो मूलमनिर्वेदः परं सुखम्। भूयस्तत्र विचेष्यामि न यत्र विचयः कृतः॥
anchor.line: Refusing to lose heart is the root of success. Look again where you have not yet looked.
anchor.translation: Not losing heart is the root of success; not losing heart is the highest happiness. I will search again, in the places I have not yet searched.
anchor.why: When you have looked everywhere, look again; giving up costs too much.

story.teaser: Hanuman searched every palace in Lanka by moonlight, and Sita was nowhere
story.for_you: Hanuman searched Lanka all night and found nothing. He was close to despair, but he told himself that refusing to lose heart is the root of success. He searched again. You have looked everywhere and found nothing yet. Refuse to let that despair win. Look again today.

script: You are carrying a heavy question. You have been trying to build your own apps for years. None have worked. Now you are working, caring for your parents, and raising children. You do not know what is wrong. You are tired and quietly questioning everything.

Arjuna stands on the battlefield. He is a warrior, and he is supposed to fight. Instead, his body is shaking. He tells Krishna that his mind is clouded. He says he cannot tell what is right. He tells Krishna he is ready to learn. And Krishna, his charioteer and guide, listens. Arjuna said:
कार्पण्यदोषोपहतस्वभावःपृच्छामि त्वां धर्मसंमूढचेताः, यच्छ्रेयः स्यान्निश्चितं ब्रूहि तन्मेशिष्यस्तेऽहं शाधि मां त्वां प्रपन्नम्.
In plain words: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.

Arjuna admits he is confused. He says his nature is weak. He asks Krishna to teach him. The texts say that clarity begins when you admit you do not know. This is easier said than done. You have been judging yourself for years. You have been telling yourself that you are failing. But Arjuna is not failing. He is simply lost. Admitting you are lost is not weakness. It is the only place where a teacher can find you.
You have been asking what is wrong with you. For today, try asking what is actually best for you. Let yourself be the student. You do not have to solve everything. You only have to be ready to learn.
What if not knowing is where the path begins?

depth.life: You are carrying a job, children, and parents, and on the side you keep trying to build apps that have not worked. The question of what is wrong has become heavy. You are tired of not knowing.
depth.points: The texts say clarity begins when you admit you do not know and ask for help. You are not failing because you are confused. You are failing because you are trying to build in a life that has no room left.
depth.practice: Sit with your phone away. Let the question of what is wrong be unanswered for one hour. Notice what happens when you stop trying to solve it.
depth.question: What would it feel like to ask for help without trying to fix yourself first?
